label: What a dollar of aid does, against cash (shared)

rows.label: Value of a dollar of humanitarian aid, as a multiple of cash to the very poor

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on charityevals' 17 humanitarian-relief models (their value per dollar before the missing-data step, at the default sliders, November 2026)
source.note: The 17 models (disaster, conflict, refugee and emergency food responses of UN-funded and private agencies) come to 0.05-0.84 times @cash.uov_per_dollar per dollar before their missing-data step, median 0.21 (0.02-0.42, median 0.12, after it). One figure for every model that values a dollar of humanitarian funding won, kept, let through or improved whose use is not known more exactly.

rows.explainer: What a dollar of humanitarian aid does, as a multiple of a dollar given as cash (@cash.uov_per_dollar). The site's own models of relief work (food, shelter, health care, water and cash in crises, by the agencies that spend most of the appeals' money) come to about a fifth of cash per dollar before their missing-data step, from a twentieth to four fifths: high delivery and security costs, goods worth less than their cost, and other funders' shares. 0.2, range 0.05 to 0.8. A model that applies it to aid it helped win applies its own missing-data step once, so at full credit it matches what the relief models say aid does.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of a rich country's aid budget (all sectors), as a multiple of cash to the very poor

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on GiveWell's values of Global Fund, Gavi and government spending (@givewell_shared.cf_value_*), the humanitarian figure above, and McIntosh and Zeitlin's cash benchmarking of a USAID programme (CEGA summary)
source.quote: the nutrition and WASH program had a positive impact on savings, a secondary outcome, but did not affect any of the primary outcomes measuring children's well-being
source.note: Mix: about a quarter global health at about 3x cash (between GiveWell's 2.1x for Gavi and 4.6x for the Global Fund, rounded down for health aid outside those two), a quarter humanitarian at 0.2x, half other development at about 0.5x (our judgment: the benchmarked programme did no better than cost-equivalent cash on its primary outcomes, a cost to USAID of $142 a household of which $114 was transferred in the cash arm; cash did better on assets and debt): 0.25 x 3 + 0.25 x 0.2 + 0.5 x 0.5 = 1.05. Low: health a sixth at GiveWell's 1.5x for government spending, humanitarian at 0.05x, development at 0.2x: 0.25 + 0.01 + 0.12 = 0.38, about 0.4. High: health a third at 4.6x, humanitarian a quarter at 0.8x, the rest at 1x: 1.53 + 0.2 + 0.42 = 2.15, about 2.

rows.explainer: What a dollar of a donor government's aid budget does when its use isn't known: the dollar a budget campaign keeps or adds, or the other aid a new pledge displaces. A mix of health aid (GiveWell values Global Fund spending at about 4.6 times cash and Gavi's at 2.1), humanitarian aid (about a fifth of cash, above) and other development aid, which cash-benchmarking trials find does about as well as its cost given as cash or less. About 1 times @cash.uov_per_dollar, range 0.4 to 2. Aid whose use is known (a vaccine pledge, a fund's own spending) takes that use's figure instead.

rows.label: Deaths averted by higher incomes in poor households, as a share of the consumption benefits
rows.explainer: Our judgment, read by every model that adds a livelihood, income or food gain abroad: higher household incomes avert some child deaths (cash transfers cut under-five deaths by about 8% in Richterman et al. 2023), and GiveWell's mortality effect for cash is about 0.2 of its consumption value. Models multiply it by the value of a life slider. 20% (0-50%).
